patient.chief_complaint: Behavioral changes, decreased novel productivity, social withdrawal — 18 months; referred by psychiatrist for 'atypical bipolar features'
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. F is a 54-year-old published novelist with a 15-year history of bipolar disorder type II (well-controlled on valproate) and hypothyroidism who is referred by his psychiatrist for neurological evaluation. His psychiatrist refers him with a note: 'progressive behavioral changes that feel different from prior bipolar episodes — patient does not recognize or endorse symptoms; consider organic process.' Over the past 18 months, Mr. F has undergone a behavioral transformation that his former partner (they divorced 2 years ago) and publisher have independently noticed. His publisher, with whom he has had a relationship for 12 years, reports that his correspondence has become strange — he sends the same paragraph from his current manuscript in every email, verbatim, regardless of the question asked. His manuscript, which he has been working on for 3 years, consists of the same 2,000 words rearranged repeatedly. He is unaware that this is unusual and insists the work is 'progressing.' He has posted a series of publicly embarrassing social media messages commenting on strangers' physical appearances and has made several sexually inappropriate advances toward his publisher's assistant, dismissing any attempt to discuss this as 'censorship.' He has developed an extraordinary fixation on a single television crime drama — watching it for 8-14 hours per day and quoting it verbatim in conversations. He is meticulous about eating the same three foods in the same sequence every day. He has lost all interest in the literary community, which was central to his identity and social world. He does not recognize any of these behaviors as problematic. His bipolar disorder has never manifested this way — his prior hypomanic episodes were characterized by rapid speech, reduced need for sleep, and increased creativity, not perseverative repetition and social disinhibition. He has no history of psychosis. His father was institutionalized in his 50s with a diagnosis of 'late-onset schizophrenia.' On brief standardized testing he presents as largely cognitively intact, with a near-normal MoCA (26/30) that contrasts with the degree of behavioral change reported by informants.

valproate.proposed: Continued valproic acid (extended release) 500 mg twice daily for bipolar disorder type II — diagnostic review of valproate level, serum ammonia, and hepatic chemistry to exclude valproate-induced hyperammonemic encephalopathy before attributing cognitive-behavioral decline to neurodegeneration
interactions: Valproate + levothyroxine: no clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction; both safe to coadminister

Valproate is a known cause of hyperammonemia even at therapeutic serum levels and with normal liver function tests, via inhibition of the urea cycle (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase) — valproate-induced hyperammonemic encephalopathy (VHE) can mimic a progressive cognitive-behavioral syndrome
contraindications: Cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., donepezil) are not indicated in frontotemporal dementia and may worsen behavioral symptoms — avoid
warnings: Serum valproate trough in this patient is within the therapeutic range (measured 68 mcg/mL; reference 50–100 mcg/mL) — no evidence of frank toxicity

Serum ammonia is only mildly elevated (38 mcg/dL; upper reference ~32 mcg/dL) and disproportionately low for the degree and 18-month duration of behavioral decline; a mild isolated elevation of this magnitude does not account for the syndrome and asymptomatic hyperammonemia is common on valproate
Hepatic chemistry (AST/ALT/bilirubin) within normal limits — no valproate hepatotoxicity

Mild valproate-associated hyperammonemia does not require discontinuation in the absence of encephalopathic features; if a contributory component were suspected, L-carnitine supplementation is the first-line measure rather than stopping a mood stabilizer that has maintained 15 years of psychiatric stability
alternatives: If valproate were implicated: L-carnitine 1 g twice daily for hyperammonemia; alternatively transition to lamotrigine or lithium with psychiatry co-management
No change to mood stabilizer is warranted on current data

results.title: Frontal-network neurodegeneration misdiagnosed as primary psychiatric disorder: clinical features and diagnostic delay

output.summary: Behavioral variant FTD is frequently misdiagnosed as bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, or personality disorder, with a mean diagnostic delay of 3-5 years. Key clinical features that should trigger neurological re-evaluation in known psychiatric patients: (1) new perseverative/stereotyped behaviors not consistent with prior psychiatric episodes; (2) severe social cognition impairment (Faux Pas, Theory of Mind) — not a feature of bipolar disorder; (3) anosognosia — patient does not recognize or endorse symptoms; (4) progressive and unremitting course rather than episodic bipolar pattern; (5) onset in 50s in previously bipolar patient. Family history of possible 'late-onset schizophrenia' in a first-degree relative may represent undiagnosed FTD. Normal MRI in a patient with behavioral syndrome should trigger FDG-PET and social cognition testing, not reassurance.

findings.finding: STANDARD TESTS (scores near normal, masking real impairment): DKEFS Trails condition 4: 16th percentile (low average but not severely impaired). Standard executive battery: 20th-30th percentile range. MoCA: 26/30 (patient asked to repeat — same score; he can focus when explicitly tested).

SOCIAL COGNITION BATTERY (severely impaired — the key diagnostic finding): Reading the Mind in the Eyes test: 14/36 (<2nd percentile — severely impaired). Faux Pas recognition: 2/10 (<2nd percentile — cannot identify social violations). Theory of Mind tasks: severely impaired (cannot attribute mental states to others). Moral decision-making tasks: utilitarian responses indicating reduced emotional resonance.

ECOLOGICAL VALIDITY TESTS (real-world judgment): Multiple Errands Task: markedly impaired — makes same errors repeatedly, does not self-correct, is unaware of errors. This captures the ecological deficit not visible on structured tests.
Language: Verbal fluency FAS: 21 words (20th percentile — low average). Naming: 54/60 BNT (40th percentile — age-appropriate). No aphasia.

output.impression: Marked dissociation between near-normal standard cognitive testing and severely impaired social cognition and ecological validity. Social cognition testing (Reading the Mind in the Eyes, Faux Pas recognition, Theory of Mind) is severely impaired (<2nd percentile), in the context of largely preserved performance on structured standard tests. Executive function is in the low-average range. Ecological validity testing demonstrates prominent real-world deficit not captured by structured instruments. Pattern of selective social-cognitive impairment with sparing on structured cognitive measures

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not indicated in the standard FTD workup once a structural MRI and FDG-PET (or amyloid PET) have characterised the lobar pattern.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

critical_actions: Recognise that subtle / normal early MRI does not exclude bvFTD; FDG-PET and genetic testing are diagnostic.
Coordinate with treating psychiatrist; distinguish bvFTD progression from bipolar relapse.
Exclude valproate-induced hyperammonemia and toxicity before attributing to neurodegeneration.
Apply Rascovsky 2011 bvFTD criteria explicitly (≥3 of 6 core features within 3 years) and document functional decline.
Assess and document decision-making, financial, and driving capacity given the high risk of impulsivity and impaired judgment in FTD.
Provide caregiver education, safety planning, and referral to FTD-focused support resources.
Offer genetic counselling and discuss cascade testing options if a pathogenic variant is identified or suspected.
contraindicated_actions: Do not start acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Do not start memantine: no evidence of benefit in bvFTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
key_reasoning_points: FTD can present with normal or subtle MRI in the first 1–2 years; FDG-PET is more sensitive (criteria pack red-herring category).
Paternal late-onset 'schizophrenia' in the 50s with institutional decline is more likely misdiagnosed FTD.
Long-standing bipolar disorder is a confounder, not the explanation, given the new informant-reported progressive trajectory.

Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: FDG-PET supports the AD-versus-FTD distinction where the clinical and structural picture is unresolved; it is not required for a diagnosis made on behavioural criteria.
